entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Raul Sevilla Manglapus (1918–1999) emerged as a pivotal figure in post-World War II Philippine politics, transitioning from a youthful anti-Japanese resistance leader to a vocal advocate for democratic reforms and national sovereignty. His career, spanning the turbulent decades of decolonization and the Marcos dictatorship, positioned him as a consistent moral voice against authoritarianism and a champion of Christian democratic ideals within Southeast Asia. He co-founded the Progressive Party of the Philippines in 1957, offering a centrist alternative to the dominant Liberal and Nacionalista parties, and later established the Christian Democratic Socialist Movement in 1968, shaping the intellectual discourse around social justice and political pluralism in the nascent republic.

Manglapus's political journey began as a delegate to the 1947 United Nations General Assembly, followed by his election to the Philippine Senate in 1961, where he championed agrarian reform and educational initiatives. His outspoken criticism of President Ferdinand Marcos's increasingly autocratic rule led to his self-exile in the United States in 1972, shortly after the declaration of Martial Law. From Washington D.C., he founded the Movement for a Free Philippines, mobilizing international opposition to the Marcos regime and testifying before the U.S. Congress on human rights abuses and the erosion of democratic institutions in his homeland. He returned triumphantly in 1986 following the People Power Revolution, subsequently serving as Secretary of Foreign Affairs under President Corazon Aquino, a role in which he negotiated the sensitive withdrawal of U.S. military bases from Clark and Subic Bay.
